title: Rear Locker Activation — Badlands and Sasquatch
tools_required: owner's manual for your model year
scan tool with Ford body and chassis coverage (only for a persistent fault)

citations.title: Bronco Nation — When to Use Bronco's Front or Rear Locker
Ford — 2021 Bronco Owner's Manual, Switching the Electronic Locking Differential On and Off (engagement table)
Ford Performance — Bronco M220 rear axle assembly with electronic locking differential (service replacement for Badlands)
The Drive — Manual Bronco Base Sasquatch Review

summary: [Every Sasquatch Bronco, the Raptor and the non-Sasquatch Badlands have both an electronic front and rear locker; the Black Diamond had a rear locker standard, and early non-Sasquatch trims could option one](https://thebronconation.com/news/when-to-use-bronco%E2%80%99s-front-or-rear-locker-t.23024/). The rear locker is a button on the dash hero switches. [Ford's 2021 owner's manual lets it engage in 2H, 4A or 4H up to 20 mph in the everyday drive modes, unlocks it automatically at 25 mph and re-locks it at 20](https://www.fordservicecontent.com/Ford_Content/vdirsnet/OwnerManual/Home/Content?variantid=7704&languageCode=en&countryCode=USA&Uid=G2114814&ProcUid=G2143784&userMarket=usa&div=f&vFilteringEnabled=False&buildtype=web). Use it when one rear tire has lost traction, and [turn it off before dry pavement](https://thebronconation.com/news/when-to-use-bronco%E2%80%99s-front-or-rear-locker-t.23024/).
description:
[Ford Performance sells the M220 rear axle with electronic locking differential as the service replacement for Badlands trucks](https://performanceparts.ford.com/part/M-4000-446B). With the locker engaged, both rear wheels turn at the same rate, so a lifted or spinning tire no longer takes all the torque and the tire with grip gets a chance to pull. An open differential, by contrast, sends power to the wheel with the least resistance.

## Do You Have One?

[Bronco Nation's rule of thumb is to count the hero switches above the center screen: at least four buttons means a rear locker, five or six means a front locker as well, and three means both differentials are open](https://thebronconation.com/news/when-to-use-bronco%E2%80%99s-front-or-rear-locker-t.23024/). No Bronco has a front locker alone.

## Engagement Conditions

[The 2021 manual's table sets the rear locker's limits by G.O.A.T. Mode](https://www.fordservicecontent.com/Ford_Content/vdirsnet/OwnerManual/Home/Content?variantid=7704&languageCode=en&countryCode=USA&Uid=G2114814&ProcUid=G2143784&userMarket=usa&div=f&vFilteringEnabled=False&buildtype=web):

- **Normal, Eco, Sport, Slippery:** 2H, 4A or 4H; engages up to 20 mph, disengages automatically at 25 mph, re-engages at 20 mph.
- **Baja, and 4L:** the table lists no speed limit.
- **Sand, Mud/Ruts and Rock Crawl:** the locker engages automatically in some ranges when you select the mode, and you can override that with the switch.

The same page says not to switch a locker on while cruise control or Trail Control is active, because the differential may have difficulty engaging. The table can change by model year, so check the electronic locking differential section of the owner's manual for your truck before relying on these numbers. If the indicator doesn't show the locker engaged, the manual's indicator and information-message pages for your year explain what the truck is telling you.

## When to Use It, and When Not To

Use the rear locker when one rear wheel is in the air or on ice or slick rock while the other has grip, on climbs where the rear is breaking traction unevenly, and [in water crossings, sand, and on inclines and declines](https://thebronconation.com/news/when-to-use-bronco%E2%80%99s-front-or-rear-locker-t.23024/). [Bronco Nation also notes that with only the rear locked on a hill, the front may pivot side to side a little more, but you still have steering to correct it](https://thebronconation.com/news/when-to-use-bronco%E2%80%99s-front-or-rear-locker-t.23024/).

[Don't use lockers on dry pavement, don't use them on a side slope with loose surfaces, and turn them off whenever you're not using them](https://thebronconation.com/news/when-to-use-bronco%E2%80%99s-front-or-rear-locker-t.23024/). A locked axle forces both wheels to the same speed, so on high-traction ground the tires scrub and the driveline binds. Don't rely on the automatic disengagement; switch it off before you return to the road.

## The Front Locker

Badlands and Sasquatch trucks also have a front locker. [It works in 4L only, engages at 20 mph or below, disengages automatically at 25 mph and re-engages at 20](https://www.fordservicecontent.com/Ford_Content/vdirsnet/OwnerManual/Home/Content?variantid=7704&languageCode=en&countryCode=USA&Uid=G2114814&ProcUid=G2143784&userMarket=usa&div=f&vFilteringEnabled=False&buildtype=web). Steering is reduced with it on, and [Bronco Nation advises against using it going downhill, on hills with a hard turn, at full steering lock, or in reverse with the wheels turned, because of the added risk to the CV joints](https://thebronconation.com/news/when-to-use-bronco%E2%80%99s-front-or-rear-locker-t.23024/). Many drivers lock the rear first and add the front only if the rear alone doesn't move the truck.
steps: Find the rear locker button on the dash hero switches.
Check the conditions for your drive mode and transfer-case range in the owner's manual: in the everyday modes that is 2H, 4A or 4H at 20 mph or below in the 2021 manual.
Make sure cruise control and Trail Control are off.
Press the rear locker button and confirm the indicator shows it engaged.
Use the locker through the obstacle.
When clear, press the button again to disengage and confirm the indicator clears before you return to pavement.
If it won't engage under the right conditions, read the owner's manual information messages for your year, then have the system scanned by a dealer or with a tool that reads Ford chassis codes.
pros: Locks the rear axle at the push of a button, on the fly, without leaving the seat.

Factory equipment on Badlands and every Sasquatch truck, [which The Drive notes adds front and rear lockers to the base model](https://www.thedrive.com/car-reviews/ford-bronco-sasquatch-manual-review).
Usable in 2H and 4H as well as 4L, per Ford's 2021 table.
cons: Dry pavement and high-traction turns wear tires and bind the driveline with the locker engaged. Always unlock before returning to road.
Some G.O.A.T. Modes engage it automatically, which can surprise you if you don't know the table.

6Gs without Badlands, Sasquatch, Black Diamond or the optional rear locker have an open rear differential; Ford Performance's route to add one is a complete M220 axle assembly plus a separate wiring and switch kit.

title: Front Brake Pad and Rotor Replacement

citations.title: Bronco6G forum — brake rotor specs and replacement thread
Bronco6G forum — torque spec reference list
Level Up Suspension — 2021+ Ford Bronco torque specs

summary: Front pads and rotors on a 6G Bronco run 1.5–2.5 hours in the driveway. Measure rotor thickness against the minimum stamped on the rotor; under that number, replace it. A forum figure we could not confirm is too wide a wear range to trust, so go by the stamp or the service manual. [Caliper bracket bolts torque to 129 Nm](https://www.bronco6g.com/forum/threads/torque-spec-reference-list.89889/) (about 95 ft-lbs).
description:
This is a safety-critical job. If you're new to brake work, read the whole procedure before starting and consider doing one side at a time so the assembled side stays as a reference. The 6G's front brakes are conventional dual-piston floating calipers — same general layout as F-150, straightforward to service, parts widely stocked.

You'll know it's time when the pad indicator squeals at low speed, the pedal feels longer than it used to, or you see less than 3mm of pad material left behind the wheel spokes. Rotor replacement is recommended any time you replace pads if the rotor is at or near minimum thickness, has heat-cracked surfaces, or has a measurable lip on the outside edge. Trail use (especially water crossings followed by hard descents) warps rotors faster than highway driving.

Pick a flat surface, chock the rear wheels, break the lug nuts loose with the wheels on the ground, then jack the front and set stands under the frame rails. Pull both front wheels. The caliper is held by two slider bolts on the back (15mm head, often with a flat to hold the slider pin); remove those and lift the caliper off — don't let it dangle by the hose, support it with a hook or zip-tie to the coil spring. Pads slide out of the bracket. To remove the rotor, the bracket bolts off (two large 21mm bolts at the back of the knuckle, 129 Nm spec). The rotor lifts free — sometimes with a tap from a dead-blow hammer if rust has welded it to the hub.

Wire-brush the hub mating surface clean — rust here is the most common cause of brake judder after a rotor swap. Set the new rotor on, hand-thread one lug nut to hold it. Bolt the bracket back on at 95 ft-lbs (129 Nm). Compress the caliper piston with a C-clamp or piston tool — open the bleeder first so old fluid pushes out into a rag rather than back into the master cylinder. Slide new pads into the bracket, lube the slider pins lightly with caliper grease, and reinstall the caliper. Torque the slider bolts to 23 ft-lbs (31 Nm).

Reinstall the wheels, [lug nuts at 150 ft-lbs (204 Nm)](https://www.levelupsuspension.com/pages/2021-ford-bronco-torque-specs) in a star pattern. Before driving, pump the brake pedal slowly until it firms up — it will feel scary-soft on the first one or two strokes after a piston compression. Bed the pads in with 8–10 stops from 35 mph down to 5 mph, then a five-minute cool-down at speed without dragging the brakes.
steps: Break lug nuts loose with the truck on the ground.
Lift the front, set jack stands under the frame.
Remove both front wheels.
Remove the two 15mm caliper slider bolts.
Lift the caliper off; hang it from the spring with a hook or zip-tie.
Slide the pads out of the bracket.
Remove the two 21mm bracket bolts; pull the bracket.
Pull the rotor (tap with a dead-blow if seized).
Wire-brush the hub face clean of rust.
Install the new rotor; hand-thread one lug nut.
Reinstall the bracket; torque to 95 ft-lbs (129 Nm).
Open the caliper bleeder; compress the piston with a C-clamp.
Install new pads with lubed slider pins.
Reinstall the caliper; torque slider bolts to 23 ft-lbs.
Close bleeder. Repeat on opposite side.
Reinstall wheels; torque lugs to 150 ft-lbs in star pattern.
Pump the brake pedal until firm before moving the truck.
Bed the pads: 8–10 stops from 35 mph to 5 mph, then cruise to cool.
pros: Conventional brake layout — no electronic parking brake retraction needed up front.
Strong aftermarket support: Centric, EBC, PowerStop, Brembo, Hawk all make 6G front kits.
95 ft-lb bracket bolt spec is reasonable — anyone with a $30 torque wrench can hit it.
cons: Brakes are safety-critical. If you've never bled a system or compressed a piston, watch a full video first and don't skip the pedal-pump step before driving.
6G rotors are larger and heavier than older Broncos — set them down carefully, not on edge.
Rotor judder after replacement almost always traces back to rust on the hub face that wasn't cleaned. Don't skip that step.

title: Engine and Cabin Air Filter Replacement

parts.name: Motorcraft FP-93 / CAF6 cabin air filter (MB3Z-19N619-A)

citations.title: CJ Pony Parts — Motorcraft FA-2022 air filter for 2.3L/2.7L Bronco
CJ Pony Parts — Motorcraft FP-93 Bronco cabin air filter
Buckle Up Off-Road — Bronco cabin air filter listing

summary: [The engine air filter is the Motorcraft FA-2022](https://www.cjponyparts.com/ford-motorcraft-air-filter-2-3l-2-7l-bronco/p/ACE39/) (2.3L and 2.7L both); [the cabin filter is the Motorcraft FP-93 / CAF6](https://www.cjponyparts.com/ford-motorcraft-cabin-air-filter-bronco/p/CAF6/). Both are 5-minute swaps with no tools beyond a flathead screwdriver — replace the engine filter every 30,000 miles and the cabin filter every 15,000, or sooner if you drive dirt.
description:
Trail dust eats air filters. A clogged engine filter robs throttle response and forces the MAF sensor to work harder; a clogged cabin filter loads the HVAC blower and pumps unfiltered desert grit into your face. Neither one is expensive to replace and both are jobs anyone can do without lifting the truck.

The engine air filter sits in a black plastic airbox on the passenger side of the engine bay, behind the headlight. Four metal spring clips hold the lid down. Pop them open (no tools — fingers, sometimes a flathead to start a stubborn clip), lift the lid, and the filter comes straight up. The FA-2022 is a flat panel rectangle — note orientation before pulling it. Wipe the airbox base clean of dust and leaves before dropping the new filter in, then snap the lid back. If you live somewhere dusty (Arizona, New Mexico, Utah trail country), an aFe Pro Dry S, K&N E-2997, or AEM Brute Force panel filter is a drop-in reusable upgrade. Don't oil reusable filters too heavily — over-oiling fouls the MAF sensor and triggers a check engine light.

The cabin filter lives behind the glove box. Open the glove box, then squeeze both sides inward to release the dampers, and let it drop fully open. A horizontal plastic door is visible on the right side of the cabin — pull the small tab to release it. The old filter slides out (it folds slightly to clear). Note the airflow arrow on the new filter — usually pointing down toward the floor — and slide it in. Close the door, reseat the glove box.

If your truck has been daily-driven on dirt roads, pull the old cabin filter outside before disposal. Pollen, pine needles, and rodent droppings shake out aggressively. Wear gloves.
steps: **Engine air filter (FA-2022):**
Open the hood. Locate the airbox on the passenger side behind the headlight.
Release the four metal spring clips around the airbox lid.
Lift the lid; remove the old filter.
Wipe the airbox base clean.
Drop in the new filter (note orientation arrow).
Reseat the lid and snap the clips closed.
**Cabin air filter (FP-93):**
Open the glove box fully.
Squeeze both glove box sides to release the dampers; let it drop.
Pull the tab on the horizontal filter access door.
Slide the old filter out (fold slightly to clear opening).
Install the new filter with the airflow arrow pointing down.
Reseat the access door and the glove box.
pros: No tools required (cabin filter); only finger-strength for the airbox clips.
Cheap parts, fast service — straightforward to bundle with an oil change.
Major impact on cabin air quality after dusty trail days.
cons: Aftermarket reusable engine filters are a real upgrade in dusty climates but require careful oiling to avoid MAF sensor faults.
Cabin filter location behind the glove box means the glove box has to be fully released — first-time owners find this awkward.
Cabin filter intervals are straightforward to forget. Set a reminder, or stack the swap with every other oil change.

title: Coolant Service Intervals — EcoBoost

citations.title: Ford Support — What engine coolant should I use
Bronco Nation — 2021 Ford Bronco recommended fluids
Bronco6G forum — coolant level diagnosis thread

summary: The 6G ships with [Motorcraft Yellow P-OAT coolant (Ford spec WSS-M97B57-A1)](https://www.ford.com/support/how-tos/more-vehicle-topics/engine-and-transmission/what-engine-coolant-should-i-use-in-my-vehicle/) rated for 10 years / 200,000 miles. Stay with Yellow. If anyone tops it off with orange, the service window collapses to 6 years / 100,000 miles. EcoBoost cooling systems trap air pockets — plan the refill carefully.
description:
Ford's published interval on the 6G is genuinely long because Yellow P-OAT is durable chemistry. The bigger risks are not interval — they're contamination, mixing, and air pockets after a refill.

The cooling system holds a few gallons depending on engine. The 2.3L EcoBoost runs roughly 2.5 gallons total. The 2.7L EcoBoost V6 runs roughly 3 gallons. Capacities are not aggressively published by Ford; the practical answer is "have a full gallon of Yellow concentrate plus a gallon of distilled, and have a second gallon staged in case you under-fill."

Two failure modes drive most coolant trouble on the 6G. First, mixing chemistries — adding orange (G-05 HOAT) or universal "green/gold/red works in any car" coolant to the yellow factory fill cuts the chemical life in half. [Use Motorcraft Yellow concentrate mixed 50/50 with distilled water](https://thebronconation.com/the-recommended-fluids-filters-and-components-of-the-2021-ford-bronco/), or buy the pre-mixed jug. Second, air pockets. EcoBoost engines (especially the 2.7L) trap air in the heater core loop. The dash will read normal temp while a pocket of air slowly cooks the cylinder head.

The bleed procedure: with engine cold, top off the degas bottle. Run the heater to MAX HEAT, fan on low. Start the engine and let it idle until the upper radiator hose is hot to the touch (thermostat open). Squeeze the upper hose periodically to burp trapped air back to the degas bottle. Top off as needed. Let it cool overnight and recheck the cold-fill line on the bottle. Expect to add half a quart over the first few heat-cool cycles.

The coolant level on the 6G is read on the degas bottle on the passenger side of the engine bay. The MIN and MAX lines are stamped into the plastic and straightforward to miss in poor light — use a flashlight at the bottle level. Low [coolant on a 6G is one of the most common forum issues](https://www.bronco6g.com/forum/threads/engine-coolant-help-found-the-level-far-below-the-minimum-line.71200/) at delivery; if your truck is consistently below MIN, look first at the upper radiator hose clamp (a known under-torqued spring clamp from the factory) and at the degas bottle cap seal.
steps: Wait until the engine is fully cold. Park level.
Remove the degas bottle cap to break vacuum on the system.
Lift the truck. Place a 3-gallon drain pan under the lower radiator hose connection.
Loosen the lower radiator hose clamp at the radiator and pull the hose. Let it drain fully (15–20 minutes).
Reinstall the lower hose, hand-tight clamp; torque clamp to spec.
Mix 50/50: half Yellow concentrate, half distilled water. Pre-mix in a clean jug.
Fill the degas bottle to MAX with the mix.
Set HVAC to MAX HEAT, fan on low. Start the engine. Idle.
As thermostat opens, squeeze the upper hose to purge air. Top off as level drops.
Run for 20–30 minutes, watching temp gauge. Shut down.
Let cool overnight. Top off to cold-fill line. Recheck after first drive cycle.
pros: Yellow P-OAT genuinely lasts 10 years if you don't contaminate it. Topping off with the wrong color is the only common reason to service early.
The degas bottle is straightforward to read. Catching low level early prevents an EcoBoost head from warping.
Distilled-water + concentrate mix is the cheapest, longest-life approach.
cons: Air pockets in the 2.7L heater core loop will eat a head if missed. The bleed procedure is not optional.
The degas bottle MIN/MAX marks are nearly flush with the bottle surface — straightforward to misread without good light.
Mixing yellow with orange (or any other chemistry) cuts service life to 6 years. There is no shortcut here.

title: Differential Fluid — Front Drive Unit (M190/M210) and Rear Axle
tools_required: ratchet and the drive or socket your fill plug takes

parts.name: Rear axle gear oil — the Motorcraft grade your owner's manual lists for your axle (about 2 qt)
Front drive unit gear oil — grade and amount per your owner's manual
Differential cover gasket or RTV (if pulling cover)

citations.title: Bronco Nation — owner's manual rear axle capacity and lubricant excerpt (63.6 oz with locker, 65.3 oz without; lists both Motorcraft 80W-90 WSP-M2C197-A and 75W-85 WSS-M2C942-A)
Ford Performance — Bronco M210 front drive unit (fits 2021-2026; notes upgrading from an M190 front drive unit)
Ford Performance — Bronco M220 rear axle assembly (service replacement for Badlands)

summary: [The rear-axle capacity table in the owner's manual, as posted on Bronco Nation, gives 63.6 fluid ounces with the electronic locking differential and 65.3 without](https://thebronconation.com/general-bronco-discussion-n.139/okay-so-got-my-diff-covr-from-jegs-but-which-fluid-help-t.8918/). The same excerpt lists two Motorcraft lubricants, an 80W-90 and a 75W-85 synthetic, and owners read it differently, so take the grade for each axle from the owner's manual for your model year or from a Ford dealer before you buy oil.
description:
The front of a 6G is an independent front drive unit, and [Ford Performance's parts list shows it can be an M190 or an M210 depending on the truck](https://performanceparts.ford.com/part/M-3002-538BF); [the Badlands rear axle is the M220](https://performanceparts.ford.com/part/M-4000-446B). Know which you have before you order fluid, a cover gasket or gears.

## Which Fluid

[The manual excerpt quoted in the Bronco Nation thread lists Motorcraft SAE 80W-90 Premium Rear Axle Lubricant (WSP-M2C197-A) and Motorcraft SAE 75W-85 Premium Synthetic Hypoid Gear Lubricant (WSS-M2C942-A) beside the rear capacity](https://thebronconation.com/general-bronco-discussion-n.139/okay-so-got-my-diff-covr-from-jegs-but-which-fluid-help-t.8918/). One member reads it as 80W-90 for the front and 75W-85 for the rear; the original poster read it the other way for a locker-equipped rear. Neither reading is settled by that excerpt, so this guide doesn't pick one: use the grade your own owner's manual assigns to each axle, or ask a Ford parts counter by VIN. Whatever you choose, meet the Ford specification number printed in the manual.

## When to Change It

Take the interval from the maintenance schedule for your model year, and change it sooner after any water crossing deep enough to reach the axle vents or if the old fluid comes out milky. An early change to clear out break-in material is optional, not a Ford requirement.

## Draining and Filling

If your axle has no drain plug, fluid removal is either through a suction pump from the fill hole or by pulling the cover. The cover route is messier but lets you wipe the magnet, look at the ring-and-pinion, and start clean.

Park level, lift the truck, and set stands so the axle stays level. Loosen the fill plug FIRST. If the fill plug won't break loose, do not drain. Once the fill plug is open, either pump fluid out from above or remove the cover bolts in a star pattern and let the cover drop. Wipe everything inside clean with a lint-free rag, clean the magnet, scrape old gasket or RTV off both sealing surfaces, lay a fresh bead of RTV looping inside the bolt holes, and bolt the cover back in a star pattern to the figure in the factory service information. Let the RTV skin per its label before filling.

Refill through the fill hole until fluid runs back out — that's the level. For the rear, expect roughly 63.6 oz with the locker or 65.3 oz without, per the manual excerpt above; for the front, take the amount from the owner's manual. Reinstall the fill plugs to the service-information torque.
steps: Lift the truck so the axle sits level; set jack stands.
Loosen the fill plug FIRST. Confirm it breaks free.
Place the drain pan under the cover.
EITHER suction fluid from the fill hole, OR remove the cover bolts in a star pattern and let the cover drop.
If the cover is off: wipe the interior clean, clean the magnet, scrape old sealant from both surfaces.
Lay an RTV bead on the cover, looping inside each bolt hole.
Reinstall the cover and torque the bolts in a star pattern to the service-information figure. Let the RTV skin.
Pump the grade your owner's manual lists into the fill hole until it runs back out.
Reinstall the fill plug to the service-information torque.
Repeat on the other axle with its own grade.
Drive 5 miles and recheck for seeps.
pros: Cleaning the magnet tells you how the axle is wearing — fine fuzz is normal; metal flakes are not.
Fresh gear oil after water crossings keeps emulsified water away from the bearings.
Basic tools only if you use the suction-pump route.
cons: The manual's fluid listing is often misread; confirm the grade for each axle before you buy.
Pulling the cover is messy. Plan for a soaked drain pan and shop floor without a layer of cardboard.
Confirming the fill plug breaks loose BEFORE draining is the most-skipped step. A stripped fill plug strands you with an empty axle.

title: Oil Change — 2.3L EcoBoost

citations.title: CJ Pony Parts — Motorcraft FL-910S for 2.3L Bronco
Bronco6G forum — upgrading the 2.3 oil filter
Ford service content — 2.3L EcoBoost capacities and specifications

summary: The 2.3L EcoBoost [takes 6.2 quarts of 5W-30 full synthetic](https://www.fordservicecontent.com/Ford_Content/vdirsnet/OwnerManual/Home/Content?variantid=3618&Uid=G1724921) with [a Motorcraft FL-910S spin-on filter](https://www.cjponyparts.com/ford-motorcraft-oil-filter-2-3l-ecoboost-bronco/p/FL910S/) — a 45-minute service that you should run every 5,000 miles on a daily-driven 6G, or every 3,000 if the truck sees real dust and water.
description:
Ford's published interval for the 2.3L EcoBoost is 10,000 miles under "normal" conditions and 5,000 under severe. If your Bronco crawls Sedona, fords Salt River, or sits parked in 110-degree Phoenix summers, you're severe service — period. Short oil intervals are cheap insurance against the carbon and fuel dilution that turbocharged direct-injection fours are known for. Run synthetic, run it on time, and you sidestep most of the headline EcoBoost failures.

The factory fluid is Motorcraft Full Synthetic 5W-30 meeting Ford spec WSS-M2C961-A1. Mobil 1 Annual Protection, Pennzoil Platinum, and Valvoline Restore & Protect in the same viscosity all meet or exceed the spec. The 2.3L is one of the more straightforward EcoBoosts to service — single inline turbo, conventional spin-on filter on the driver-side of the block, drain plug visible from below.

Park on level ground and run the engine 5 minutes to warm the oil. Shut down, lift the front, and set jack stands under the frame. Crawl under, pull the engine splash shield (eight 8mm bolts and two push pins), and the drain plug sits at the rear of the pan — 13mm hex, ~22 ft-lbs of torque with a fresh crush washer. Drain takes 3–5 minutes. Spin the FL-910S off by hand or with a strap wrench, wipe the sealing surface clean, smear a film of fresh oil on the new filter's gasket, and hand-tighten three-quarters of a turn past first contact. Refill with 6.2 quarts, run the engine 30 seconds, recheck the dipstick after settling, and inspect for leaks before dropping the truck.

Reset the oil life monitor through the SYNC instrument cluster menu: Settings → Vehicle → Oil Life Reset → Hold OK.
steps: Warm the engine 5 minutes, then shut off.
Lift the front and set jack stands under the frame rails.
Remove the engine splash shield (8mm bolts + push pins).
Position a drain pan; remove the drain plug (13mm).
While draining, spin off the FL-910S filter.
Install the new filter with oiled gasket, hand-tighten 3/4 turn past contact.
Replace the drain plug with new crush washer, torque to 22 ft-lbs.
Reinstall the splash shield.
Lower the truck. Add 6.2 quarts of 5W-30 full synthetic.
Start engine for 30 seconds, shut off, wait one minute, check dipstick, top to full.
Reset the oil life monitor through SYNC.
pros: Straightforward service — no special tools beyond a 13mm and a strap wrench.
The FL-910S filter is cheap (~$12) and stocked at every parts counter.
Quality synthetic at 5,000-mile intervals heads off most known EcoBoost problems.
cons: The splash shield adds 5 minutes vs older trucks with open underbodies.
Direct-injection EcoBoosts can dilute oil with fuel — stretching intervals to 10K is asking for problems on a hard-used truck.
Mishandling the crush washer or over-torquing the drain plug into the aluminum pan is an expensive mistake. Stick to the 22 ft-lb spec.

title: Oil Change — 2.7L EcoBoost V6
tools_required: 24mm or 27mm cap wrench for cartridge housing

citations.title: CJ Pony Parts — Motorcraft FL-2062A cartridge filter for 2.7L Bronco
Bronco Nation — recommended fluids, filters, and components for the 2021 Bronco
Autoevolution — 2021 Ford Bronco engine oil change guide

summary: The 2.7L EcoBoost V6 takes 7.0 quarts of 5W-30 full synthetic with [a Motorcraft FL-2062A cartridge filter](https://www.cjponyparts.com/ford-motorcraft-oil-filter-cartridge-2-7l-bronco/p/FL2062A/) — a 60-minute service that the cartridge housing makes a touch finickier than the 2.3L's spin-on.
description:
The 2.7L "Nano" V6 in the Outer Banks, Badlands, and Wildtrak Broncos is a strong engine — twin-turbo direct-injection V6 with port injection added, plenty of low-end torque, and proven across the F-150 program since 2015. Treat it like any other modern boosted gasoline V6: full synthetic, 5,000-mile intervals if you do any off-road work or live somewhere hot, and don't run cheap fluid. There is an active 2.7L EcoBoost engine knock lawsuit covering certain 2021–2022 builds — keeping documented oil-change records protects you if a warranty claim becomes necessary.

The factory fill is [Motorcraft Full Synthetic 5W-30 to spec WSS-M2C961-A1](https://thebronconation.com/the-recommended-fluids-filters-and-components-of-the-2021-ford-bronco/). The filter is a cartridge, not a spin-on — it lives in a plastic-topped housing on the top of the engine, driver side, between the intake and the firewall. The cap takes a 24mm or 27mm cap wrench depending on production date. Replace the housing O-ring every other service (it ships in the FL-2062A box).

Park on level ground and warm the engine 5 minutes. Pop the hood, locate the filter housing, and remove the cap with the cap wrench — pull the old cartridge straight up. Wipe the housing clean. Down below, raise the front, set stands, pull the splash shield (8mm bolts and push pins), and remove the 13mm drain plug at the rear of the oil pan. Let it drain a full five minutes — the V6 pan holds more than the 2.3L and the last quart matters. Reinstall the drain plug with a new crush washer at 22 ft-lbs.

Drop the new cartridge into the housing, install a fresh O-ring on the cap, and torque the cap to 18 ft-lbs (it will click into a hard stop — don't crank it). Refill with 7.0 quarts of 5W-30 synthetic. Start the engine, watch the oil pressure light extinguish in under three seconds, run it 30 seconds, shut down, and check the dipstick after a one-minute settle. Reset the oil life monitor through SYNC.
steps: Warm engine 5 minutes, then shut off.
Open hood. Locate the cartridge filter housing on top of the engine.
Remove the cap with cap wrench (24 or 27mm); lift out the old cartridge.
Lift the front and set jack stands.
Remove the splash shield (8mm + push pins).
Drain through the 13mm pan plug onto a pan; wait 5 minutes.
Install drain plug with new crush washer at 22 ft-lbs.
Reinstall splash shield. Lower the truck.
Drop new FL-2062A cartridge into housing.
Install new O-ring on cap; reinstall cap and torque to 18 ft-lbs.
Refill with 7.0 quarts of 5W-30 full synthetic.
Start engine; verify oil pressure light goes out under 3 seconds.
Run 30 seconds, shut off, recheck dipstick after 1 minute.
Reset oil life monitor in SYNC.
pros: Cartridge filters are environmentally cleaner (you only throw away the paper element) and let you inspect for metal contamination on every service.
7-quart sump and synthetic oil give the 2.7L a generous thermal margin off-road.
Documented oil records strengthen any future warranty claim, including the 2.7L knock action.
cons: Cap wrench is an extra tool most new owners don't already have (~$15).
Over-torquing the plastic filter cap will crack it — stay at 18 ft-lbs.
The cartridge housing is wedged between intake and firewall; large hands struggle without a deep socket or wrench extension.

title: Transfer Case Fluid Service

citations.title: BlauParts — 2024-2025 Ford Bronco Transfer Case Fluid Change Kit
Bronco6G forum — Transfer Case Fluid Change

summary: The 6G transfer case takes 1.2–1.6 quarts of [MERCON LV ATF (Ford spec WSS-M2C938-A)](https://www.blauparts.com/ford-bronco-transfer-case-differential-oil-change-kit-ravenol.html). Capacity depends on which 4x4 system you have — Part-Time 4x4 is 1.2 L (1.3 qt), Advanced 4x4 with 4A mode is 1.55 L (1.6 qt). Ford lists no scheduled service. Trail-driven trucks should change it at 30,000 miles or after any water crossing that touched the case vent.
description:
The transfer case is one of the most ignored fluids on the truck because Ford never tells you to change it. Trail use changes the math — heat, water, and shock loading thrash ATF. Plan a first service at 30,000 miles and every 30,000 after, with an extra dump if you fully submerged the case crossing water.

Use the correct fluid. The transfer case wants Motorcraft MERCON LV (WSS-M2C938-A), not gear oil. Substituting heavier oil destroys the clutch pack in the 4A actuator. Stay with the spec.

The case sits behind the transmission with the fill plug high on the rear face and the drain plug on the bottom. Both are 10mm Allen-head (hex socket) plugs. Loosen the fill plug FIRST — if it won't break loose, do not drain. Once the fill plug spins free, position your drain pan, remove the drain plug, and let it run. Expect about a quart out, no matter which 4x4 system you have, because ATF clings to the case internals.

Reinstall the drain plug torqued to roughly 20 ft-lbs (the service manual lists 27 N·m). [Pump fresh MERCON LV into the fill hole](https://www.bronco6g.com/forum/threads/transfer-case-fluid-change.82715/) until it weeps back out — that's the correct level. The case fills from the side, so do not overfill chasing a measured capacity. Reinstall the fill plug at the same torque. Drive 5 miles and recheck for seep.

If your truck has Advanced 4x4 (the 4A "auto" mode), the case has a clutch pack that engages and disengages while driving. Old or contaminated fluid in that pack causes hesitation when 4A swaps drive between front and rear axles. Owners who notice a brief shudder when 4A is selected typically fix it with a fluid swap.
steps: Park level. Lift the truck so the case sits level. Set jack stands.
Identify the fill plug (high on rear face) and drain plug (bottom). Both are 10mm hex.
Loosen the fill plug FIRST. Do not crack the drain until the fill plug spins.
Position drain pan. Remove the drain plug. Let it drain 10 minutes.
Inspect old fluid — milky means water intrusion; metal flakes mean clutch wear.
Reinstall drain plug at ~20 ft-lbs.
Pump fresh MERCON LV into the fill hole until it weeps back out the threads.
Reinstall fill plug at ~20 ft-lbs.
Drive 5 miles and recheck both plugs for seep.
pros: Cheap insurance — two quarts of ATF and an hour heads off a $4,000 transfer case rebuild.
Detects water intrusion early. Milky fluid after a crossing tells you the vent or seals need attention before the case grenades.
The job uses basic tools. No specialty equipment, no shop visit.
cons: Ford gives no scheduled interval, so it gets skipped by every owner who only does what the dash tells them.
4A "auto" mode trucks are pickier about fluid quality than Part-Time-only trucks; old fluid causes engagement shudder.
The fill plug threads bite hard. Use anti-seize sparingly on reinstall so the next service isn't a fight.

title: HOSS Suspension Overview — Four Levels, Sasquatch vs Base
tools_required: owner's manual for your model year

citations.title: Bronco Nation — Bronco's Boss HOSS System: 4 Levels of Performance
Autoblog — Ford Bronco Suspension Deep Dive
ShockSurplus — Ultimate Ford Bronco Shocks & Suspension Guide
Bronco Nation — Shocks to the System: Understanding Bronco's Four Levels of HOSS
Motor1 — 2022 Bronco Wildtrak gets HOSS 3.0 package
Bronco Nation — When to Use Bronco's Front or Rear Locker
The Drive — Ford recalls 150,000 Broncos over rear shock reservoirs (25V-025)

summary: [Ford ships the 6G with four distinct HOSS suspension levels](https://thebronconation.com/broncos-boss-hoss-system-4-levels-of-performance/). HOSS 1.0 (Base, Big Bend, Outer Banks, Black Diamond) runs twin-tube shocks. HOSS 2.0 (Badlands, Everglades, Heritage, the First Edition, Wildtraks built without the HOSS 3.0 package, and any Sasquatch-package truck) runs Bilstein position-sensitive monotubes with external reservoirs and end-stop control. [HOSS 3.0 is the FOX 2.5 internal-bypass package, optional on the 2022 Wildtrak and standard on the 2023 Wildtrak; HOSS 4.0 is the Bronco Raptor's FOX 3.1 Live Valve setup, standard since the 2022 model year](https://thebronconation.com/news/shocks-to-the-system-understanding-bronco%E2%80%99s-four-levels-of-hoss-performance-t.19812/). Knowing which one is under your truck dictates what aftermarket parts actually fit.
description:
The HOSS naming gets confusing because trim level and shock package don't always match. Sasquatch is a package, not a trim — you can order Sasquatch on a Base, Big Bend, Outer Banks, Wildtrak, or Badlands. Sasquatch automatically pulls in the Bilstein HOSS 2.0 dampers, the 35-inch Goodyear tires, the high-clearance fender flares, the 4.7 final drive, and the front and rear electronic lockers. Badlands trim includes the same Bilstein dampers and, [even without Sasquatch, both front and rear lockers](https://thebronconation.com/news/when-to-use-bronco%E2%80%99s-front-or-rear-locker-t.23024/).

HOSS 1.0 (Base, Big Bend, Outer Banks, Black Diamond without Sasquatch) runs twin-tube shocks tuned more for on-road compliance than articulation. The truck still drives well off-road but tops out earlier and lacks the bottom-out resistance for high-speed dirt. Aftermarket replacement is manageable and cheap because you're swapping common twin-tube geometry.

HOSS 2.0 is the part you actually want for any meaningful off-road use. [The Bilstein position-sensitive end-stop control valve (ESCV) dampers stiffen progressively](https://www.autoblog.com/features/ford-bronco-suspension-deep-dive) as the shock approaches full compression or full extension — that's what "position-sensitive" means. The middle of the travel range is plush; the last inch on either end ramps up hydraulic resistance to prevent metal-on-metal bottom-out. The remote reservoirs add oil volume so the shock doesn't fade under sustained high-frequency work.

HOSS 3.0 is the Wildtrak's step up: [FOX 2.5-inch internal-bypass dampers, revised spring rates, and a severe-duty steering rack and tie rod ends](https://www.motor1.com/news/569210/ford-bronco-wildtrak-hoss-package/). HOSS 4.0 is Bronco Raptor-only — FOX 3.1 Live Valve internal-bypass shocks with electronically variable damping. Different mounts, different geometry, not a drop-in for non-Raptor trucks.

There is a recall on HOSS 2.0 trucks: [NHTSA 25V-025 covers about 150,000 2021–2024 Broncos with the Badlands trim or Sasquatch package](https://www.thedrive.com/news/ford-recalls-150000-broncos-because-part-of-the-rear-suspension-can-fall-off), because corrosion between the external reservoir, its mounting flange, and the damper body on the long-flange Bilstein rear shocks can let the reservoir separate. If you bought a used Badlands or Sasquatch, confirm the recall was performed by entering your VIN at ford.com/support.

The aftermarket replacement question depends on what you're trying to do. [For HOSS 1.0 trucks, dropping in HOSS 2.0 Bilsteins or aftermarket monotubes](https://www.shocksurplus.com/blogs/news/ultimate-ford-bronco-shock-buying-guide) (Icon, Old Man Emu, Zone, RPG) is a real upgrade. For HOSS 2.0 trucks, stay with Bilsteins or step up to Fox 2.5 / King 2.5 if you're chasing high-speed desert capability — there's no point downgrading to a generic monotube.
steps: Check your build sheet or window sticker for "HOSS" or "Sasquatch."
Look at the rear shocks: an external reservoir = HOSS 2.0, 3.0 or 4.0; plain twin-tube body = HOSS 1.0.

Check the dash hero switches. Locker buttons indicate a Badlands, Sasquatch, Raptor, Black Diamond, or a truck optioned with the rear locker; a sway-disconnect button indicates Badlands or First Edition.
Run your VIN at ford.com/support to confirm any shock-related recalls have been performed.
Plan modifications based on what you have — don't buy 37s on HOSS 1.0 without upgrading the dampers first.
pros: Knowing which HOSS package you have prevents wasted aftermarket spending.
HOSS 2.0 Bilsteins are genuinely well-engineered factory dampers — many trucks need no shock upgrade until 50,000+ miles or until going to 37s.
Position-sensitive damping gives you a softer on-road ride and stiffer end-stops than any single-rate shock could.
cons: HOSS 1.0 trucks need a shock upgrade before any aggressive off-road use. The factory twin-tubes fade fast.
The HOSS 2.0 recall affected a lot of trucks — verify before buying used.
HOSS 4.0 (Raptor) parts are not cross-compatible with HOSS 2.0 or 3.0; they share a name and not much else.

title: Sway Bar Disconnect — Badlands Feature
tools_required: scan tool with Ford body and chassis coverage (only for a persistent fault)

citations.title: Ford Support — How to disconnect the front stabilizer bar
Bronco Nation — 2021 Front Stabilizer Bar Disconnection How-To (4H/4L, under 20 mph, standby above 20, Rock Crawl auto-disconnect)

summary: The electronic front stabilizer-bar disconnect, which [Ford lists as standard and only available on the First Edition and Badlands](https://www.ford.com/support/how-tos/more-vehicle-topics/engine-and-transmission/bronco-how-to-disconnect-the-front-stabilizer-bar/), is a button on the dash hero-switch bank. [In 4H or 4L, below 20 mph, the bar disconnects and an amber bar icon lights; above 20 mph it reconnects and a gray icon shows the system is on standby](https://www.ford.com/support/how-tos/more-vehicle-topics/engine-and-transmission/bronco-how-to-disconnect-the-front-stabilizer-bar/), ready to disconnect again when you slow down. It costs nothing to use and frees the front wheels to articulate.
description:
The button sits with the other off-road hero switches on the instrument panel; Ford includes it in the Off-Road Hero Switch Pack on the trims that have it. Press it once to turn the system on.

## How the System Behaves

Ford's support page describes three states. **Off**: the bar is connected and the truck drives normally. **Disconnected** (amber bar icon): you are in 4H or 4L below 20 mph, and the front wheels can articulate further than the connected bar allows, so one tire can drop into a hole while the other climbs. **Standby** (gray bar icon): the system is on but the truck is above 20 mph, so the bar has reconnected; [it disconnects again once you drop back below the speed threshold](https://www.ford.com/support/how-tos/more-vehicle-topics/engine-and-transmission/bronco-how-to-disconnect-the-front-stabilizer-bar/).

The conditions are the transfer-case range and the speed. If the button does nothing, confirm you are in 4H or 4L and below 20 mph. Ford doesn't describe the mechanism on its support page, and this guide doesn't either; for anything beyond operation, the owner's manual and the factory service information for your model year are the references.

## Reconnecting, Drive Modes, and Rock Crawl

Reconnect by pressing the button again. [The system also switches off when you shift out of 4H or 4L, when the engine is switched off, or when you select a drive mode that doesn't allow the bar to disconnect](https://www.ford.com/support/how-tos/more-vehicle-topics/engine-and-transmission/bronco-how-to-disconnect-the-front-stabilizer-bar/). Ford notes the feature is not available in certain G.O.A.T. Modes. The exception runs the other way in [Rock Crawl, where the bar disconnects automatically](https://thebronconation.com/2021-ford-bronco-front-stabilizer-bar-disconnection-how-to/) without the button.

The standby behavior is the safety net: you can't drive at highway speed with the bar disconnected, because it reconnects above 20 mph on its own.

## Trims Without the Button

[Ford lists the disconnect only for the First Edition and Badlands](https://www.ford.com/support/how-tos/more-vehicle-topics/engine-and-transmission/bronco-how-to-disconnect-the-front-stabilizer-bar/); [Bronco Nation notes the Wildtrak, for one, does not have it](https://thebronconation.com/2021-ford-bronco-front-stabilizer-bar-disconnection-how-to/). Ford has moved features between packages across model years, so check the window sticker on a later truck rather than assuming by trim name. On a truck without the button, any disconnect is an aftermarket part: check that its maker lists your trim and model year before buying.

The factory disconnect works on the front stabilizer bar only.

## If It Won't Disconnect

If the amber icon never lights in 4H or 4L below 20 mph, and you are not in a G.O.A.T. Mode that blocks it, treat it as a fault rather than operator error. Check the owner's manual for the warning messages your model year shows, then have the system scanned with a tool that reads Ford body and chassis codes, or take it to a dealer.
steps: Find the stabilizer-bar disconnect button on the dash hero switches.
Shift to 4H or 4L. Slow below 20 mph.
Press the button once. The amber bar icon means the bar is disconnected.
Use the disconnect through the obstacle. Above 20 mph the bar reconnects and the gray standby icon shows; it disconnects again when you slow below 20.
When done, press the button again, shift out of 4H/4L, or switch off the engine to turn the system off.
In Rock Crawl, expect the bar to disconnect automatically.
If the amber icon never lights under the right conditions, check the owner's manual and have the system scanned.
pros: More front-wheel articulation off-road at the push of a button, with no tools.
You can disconnect without stopping and crawling under the truck.
Automatic reconnect above 20 mph prevents driving at speed with the bar loose.
cons: First Edition and Badlands only, per Ford. Other trims need an aftermarket solution.
Not available in every G.O.A.T. Mode, which can look like a fault if you don't know it.
Diagnosing a real fault takes a scan tool that reads Ford chassis codes, or a dealer visit.
